title: US rally, Euro gains and Asian upside set tone for Indian open
excerpt: Global equities closed higher on Friday while US yields rose and the rupee weakened. Indian indices opened lower, with banks and auto lagging but IT and metals holding up. Today's focus is on earnings, RBI data and US inflation cues.

What happened

India

The Nifty 50 closed at 25,607.20 points, down 0.82% on Friday, while the Sensex slipped to 83,339.26 points, a 0.71% decline. The Nifty Bank fell 1.04% to 63,040.90 points and the Nifty IT rose 1.71% to 32,758.10 points. The India VIX dropped 6.37% to 16.55 points, signalling reduced market fear. Across the NSE, Financials fell 1.21% to 30,279.70 points, PSU Bank down 1.08% to 9,491.80 points, Auto slid 2.16% to 28,199.90 points, Pharma was flat at 28,973.55 points, FMCG dropped 1.86% to 49,212.45 points, Metal rose 2.59% to 11,878.00 points, Energy gained 0.72% to 36,935.00 points and Realty advanced 1.80% to 958.95 points. The broad weakness was anchored by higher US yields and a weaker rupee.

Banking stocks led the downside, with the Nifty Bank down 1.04% and the Financials index down 1.21%, reflecting pressure from rising US Treasury yields that pushed the 10‑year to 4.94%. The rupee weakened to 92.98 per dollar, adding import‑cost concerns for lenders. Despite the stress, the India VIX fell 6.37%, suggesting that market participants were not yet pricing in heightened volatility. The IT sector bucked the trend, posting a 1.71% gain, while metals posted a solid 2.59% rise, supported by global commodity optimism. Energy’s modest 0.72% gain and Realty’s 1.80% rise offered limited defensive support.

The sector spread highlighted a classic risk‑on/risk‑off split. IT’s 1.71% rise to 32,758.10 points and Metal’s 2.59% jump to 11,878.00 points indicated continued appetite for growth and commodity‑linked stocks. Energy’s 0.72% gain to 36,935.00 points and Realty’s 1.80% rise to 958.95 points provided modest defensive cushioning. Conversely, Auto’s 2.16% fall to 28,199.90 points and FMCG’s 1.86% drop to 49,212.45 points reflected sensitivity to consumer spending amid a weaker rupee. Pharma’s near‑flat performance at 28,973.55 points suggested limited catalyst impact. The overall market breadth was uneven, with volatility easing as the VIX fell to 16.55 points.

Going into today’s session, the Nifty 50 is likely to open lower, given Friday’s 0.82% decline and the rupee’s weakness at 92.98 per dollar. The higher US 10‑year yield at 4.94% may keep foreign inflows restrained, while the subdued VIX at 16.55 points could limit immediate panic but leaves room for a quick spike if yields rise further. Sector momentum points to a cautious start: banks and auto may stay under pressure, while IT and metals could provide the only upside. Traders should watch the opening of US Treasury futures and any RBI commentary for clues on short‑term direction.

Global markets

US equity markets closed sharply higher on Friday, with the S&P 500 up 1.60% to 7,297.49 points, the Nasdaq climbing 2.31% to 24,129.50 points and the Dow Jones gaining 1.18% to 50,774.94 points. In Europe, the FTSE 100 rose 0.84% to 10,698.81 points, reinforcing the risk‑on tone. Asian benchmarks also posted gains, as the Nikkei 225 advanced 2.11% to 58,711.11 points and Hong Kong’s Hang Seng rose 2.11% to 22,694.77 points. The coordinated rally across regions suggested renewed confidence in growth stocks, even as monetary tightening loomed.

The rally unfolded alongside a 1.82% rise in the US 10‑year Treasury yield, which settled at 4.94%, indicating tighter monetary expectations. The dollar strengthened 0.59% against the rupee, closing at 92.98 INR per USD, adding pressure on emerging‑market currencies. Safe‑haven assets also rallied: gold jumped 2.91% to $3,668.50 per ounce and Brent crude edged up 0.22% to $90.84 a barrel. Bitcoin, trading live, rose 0.35% to $60,073.91, reflecting modest crypto optimism that mirrored the equity surge.

The global equity surge was driven by optimism around artificial‑intelligence earnings and a softer outlook on inflation, yet the simultaneous rise in yields and the dollar introduced a counterweight. Asian markets mirrored the US upside, suggesting that the risk appetite could spill over into the Indian session. However, the higher cost of capital implied by the 4.94% US yield may temper enthusiasm for growth‑oriented stocks, while the weaker rupee could amplify import‑related pressures on Indian corporates.

Rupee, rates and commodities

The rupee closed at 92.98 per dollar, a 0.59% weakening that reflects the dollar’s recent strength. Higher US Treasury yields, now at 4.94%, are likely to keep capital outflows in check, pressuring Indian equities, especially import‑heavy sectors. Brent crude’s modest rise to $90.84 a barrel supports energy stocks but also adds to inflationary concerns. Gold’s 2.91% jump to $3,668.50 per ounce signals safe‑haven demand, which could divert funds from risk assets. Together, these macro forces set a cautious backdrop for the Indian market, with the weaker rupee and higher yields weighing on sentiment.

Cryptocurrency markets showed limited impact on Indian equities, with Bitcoin trading live up 0.35% to $60,073.91, indicating modest risk appetite among global investors. Gold’s rise to $3,668.50 per ounce may attract Indian investors seeking a hedge against currency depreciation, potentially boosting domestic bullion demand. Oil’s slight increase to $90.84 a barrel offers a modest tailwind for energy stocks but also raises input costs for manufacturers. The combination of a stronger dollar, higher yields, and rising precious‑metal prices creates a mixed macro environment that could see risk assets under pressure while defensive assets gain appeal.

Overall, the macro backdrop points to a restrained opening for Indian markets. The rupee’s weakness at 92.98 and the 4.94% US 10‑year yield suggest that foreign inflows may be limited, especially for sectors reliant on external funding. Energy and metal stocks could benefit from commodity price support, while banks and auto manufacturers may feel the squeeze from higher financing costs and a softer currency. Low volatility, as indicated by the India VIX at 16.55 points, may keep trading calm unless yields climb further, at which point volatility could spike and reshape intra‑day dynamics.

News that matters

  1. Dollar Rises Toward Best Monthly Streak Since 2024 on AI Risk

    Mint

    The dollar climbed toward its longest monthly winning streak in two years as a rupture in the artificial intelligence trade and rising interest rates spurred demand for safe-haven assets. This matters because a stronger dollar typically puts pressure on emerging market currencies and can weigh on Indian equity sentiment by making foreign capital flows more selective. Assets such as the rupee and export-oriented equities are most affected, while safe-haven demand may support gold. The picture would change if US rate expectations ease or if the AI trade rupture resolves, which could halt the dollar's advance and relieve pressure on emerging markets. The detail on the exact magnitude of the monthly streak beyond the two-year reference is not yet known from the provided summary.

  2. Wall St Week Ahead Volatile stock market confronts jobs data, rate view as next tests

    Reuters

    Wall Street is set to confront volatile market conditions alongside upcoming jobs data and the next view on interest rates. This matters because employment figures and central bank guidance directly influence the trajectory of US yields, which in turn affect the cost of capital and the attractiveness of Indian assets to foreign investors. Sectors sensitive to interest rates, such as financials and real estate, along with the broader Nifty and Bank Nifty, could see heightened volatility depending on the outcome. The picture would change if the jobs data comes in significantly softer or harder than expected, or if the rate view shifts toward a more hawkish or dovish stance. Specific consensus forecasts for the jobs report are not provided in the available detail.

  3. OPEC+ set to keep oil production targets steady: Report

    Economic Times

    OPEC+ is expected to maintain its production targets for Q1 2027 despite conflicting member production estimates and the ongoing Iran conflict, while reassessing capacity data amid concerns over initial findings. Analysts foresee a potential global oil surplus next year, which increases pressure on the group. This matters because Brent crude closed at 90.84 USD per barrel, and any shift in supply expectations directly impacts energy sector valuations and inflation-linked inputs for Indian industry. The Energy sector index, which closed at 36935.00 points, is particularly exposed. The picture would change if OPEC+ decides to cut output or if geopolitical tensions in Iran escalate sharply, disrupting supply. The exact production figures for individual members remain unknown from the summary.

  4. Copper sweeps higher as China offers stock market support

    Economic Times

    Copper prices experienced a notable increase after China's cabinet announced support for its stock market, following a significant drop earlier in the month. China's industrial profits recorded their highest growth in five months during October, and the Yangshan premium reflects robust import demand. This matters because copper is a key industrial input, and its price trajectory affects global manufacturing costs and commodity-linked equities. In India, the Metal sector index closed at 11878.00 points, indicating direct sensitivity to base metal price moves. The picture would change if China's stock market support fails to stabilize sentiment or if industrial profit growth decelerates in subsequent data. The exact magnitude of the copper price increase beyond the directional move is not yet known.

  5. Gold pares gains as Fed hike risks linger, eyes first weekly rise in three weeks

    Mint

    Gold pared gains on Friday while bullion remained on track for its first weekly rise in three weeks, even as Fed hike risks lingered in the background. Spot silver climbed 4.4% to 43.30 USD per ounce. This matters because Gold closed at 3668.50 USD per troy ounce, and any sustained move affects import bills and portfolio allocation for Indian investors. Assets such as the India VIX, which closed at 16.55 points, often correlate with safe-haven demand. The picture would change if the Federal Reserve signals a more hawkish rate path, which could cap precious metal gains. The exact weekly percentage change for gold is not provided in the summary.

  6. Gold prices rise in India and China after hitting 15-month low as physical demand improves despite global rate concerns

    Mint

    Gold prices rose in India and China after hitting a 15-month low as physical demand improved despite global rate concerns. This matters because the metal's recovery from a 15-month low influences domestic consumer demand and import dynamics for a country that is a major buyer. The improvement in physical demand supports the price level of 3668.50 USD per troy ounce seen in the global close. Sectors and assets linked to bullion, including jewellery and mining stocks, are affected. The picture would change if global rate concerns intensify or if physical demand weakens in subsequent sessions. The exact percentage gain in India and China is not provided.

  7. Bitcoin slips back below $60,000, missing out on Wall Street rally from Thanksgiving break

    Mint

    Bitcoin slipped back below 60000 USD, missing out on the Wall Street rally from the Thanksgiving break. The divergence was particularly notable given that Bitcoin had advanced alongside US equity futures earlier in the day. This matters because Bitcoin is trading live at 60073.91 USD, and a failure to hold above the 60000 USD threshold signals weakness in risk-on sentiment that often accompanies Indian equity rallies. The divergence from US equity futures suggests that crypto may be decoupling from traditional market cues, affecting allocation decisions for Indian investors. The picture would change if Bitcoin regains momentum above 60000 USD and aligns with US equity futures again. The exact timing of the slip relative to the futures move is not specified.

Our view

cautious Analyst board aligned (3 of 3 views)

The board remains cautious. US equity benchmarks closed with solid gains – the S&P 500 rose 1.60% to 7,297.49, the Nasdaq added 2.31% to 24,129.50 and the Dow Jones climbed 1.18% to 50,774.94. Europe followed, the FTSE 100 up 0.84% to 10,698.81. In Asia, the Nikkei 225 and Hang Seng each jumped about 2.1%, signalling a risk‑on tone. Yet Indian markets slipped: the Nifty 50 fell 0.82% to 25,607.20 and the Nifty Bank dropped 1.04% to 63,040.90. The rupee weakened to 92.98 per dollar (+0.59%) and the US 10‑year yield rose to 4.94% (+1.82%). These mixed signals justify a cautious stance ahead of the open.

Sector breadth was uneven. The IT index rose 1.71% to 32,758.10, providing a clear upside driver, while Metal outperformed with a 2.59% gain to 11,878.00 and Energy added 0.72% to 36,935.00. Auto fell 2.16% to 28,199.90 and FMCG slipped 1.86% to 49,212.45, underscoring consumer‑sensitive weakness. Financials dropped 1.21% to 30,279.70 and PSU Bank slipped 1.08% to 9,491.80, reflecting pressure on lenders from a weaker rupee and higher US yields. Pharma was flat at 28,973.55 and Realty rose 1.80% to 958.95. The India VIX fell 6.37% to 16.55, indicating reduced volatility despite the mixed equity performance.

Valuation metrics suggest upside potential. A recent CIO note highlighted that large‑cap valuations sit at historic lows, implying room for a rally if risk appetite improves. However, funding costs are rising: the US 10‑year yield is now 4.94% and the rupee is at 92.98 per dollar, both of which increase borrowing costs for Indian corporates and weigh on financial stocks. The combination of cheap valuations and higher external financing pressures creates a balanced risk‑reward profile, reinforcing the board’s cautious outlook until clearer direction emerges from domestic data and global yield trends.

Today's market will be shaped by several near‑term catalysts. Indian investors will watch the RBI’s policy meeting for any shift in rate stance, while the release of CPI and industrial production data will test inflationary pressures. On the corporate side, earnings from the IT sector are due, which could validate the sector’s recent strength. Globally, US non‑farm payrolls and the Fed’s minutes will influence the 10‑year yield trajectory. Together, these events will determine whether the risk‑on bias from Asian markets can translate into a stronger Indian open or whether domestic headwinds will keep the market subdued.

Sector calls

AutounderweightAuto declined 2.16% to 28,199.90, indicating consumer‑spending weakness and exposure to higher financing costs, warranting a defensive stance.

What would change our view

A sudden reversal in global risk sentiment, such as a sharp pull‑back in US equities or a rapid decline in US yields, could lift the rupee and spark a broader rally in Indian equities, undermining the cautious view.

If domestic data surprise on the upside – for example, stronger‑than‑expected CPI, robust industrial production, or better‑than‑forecast corporate earnings – the market could shift into a risk‑on mode, rendering the cautious stance too defensive.

Geopolitical developments that trigger a commodity‑price surge, especially in metals and energy, could boost sectoral leaders and offset financial‑sector weakness, leading to a more bullish market environment than anticipated.

How the analyst board voted
  • Momentum strategist: cautious, conviction 3/5. US equities closed strongly (+1% to +2%) and Asian markets (Nikkei, Hang Seng) jumped ~2%, bolstering global risk appetite and supporting a potential bounce in India. Indian breadth is mixed: Nifty (-0.82%) and Bank Nifty (-1.04%) lag, but sectoral leaders like IT (+1.71%), Metal (+2.59%) and Energy (+0.72%) are up, while India VIX fell 6.37%, indicating reduced volatility. The rupee weakened (USD/INR +0.59%) amid a stronger dollar, which could pressure import‑heavy stocks and offset some of the global risk‑on bias.
  • Risk manager: cautious, conviction 3/5. US and European markets posted strong gains (+1.6% to +2.31%) while Indian indices closed lower (Nifty -0.82%, Nifty Bank -1.04%), hinting at domestic weakness despite global risk appetite. USD/INR rose to 92.98 (+0.59%) and US 10Y yields jumped to 4.94% (+1.82%), increasing funding cost pressures on Indian equities and the rupee. India VIX fell 6.37% to 16.55, indicating reduced volatility, and large‑cap valuations are at historic lows, offering upside potential that tempers the downside risk.
  • Macro economist: cautious, conviction 3/5. Global risk‑on sentiment (S&P +1.6%, Nasdaq +2.3%, Nikkei +2.1%) supports equities, yet Indian indices slipped (Nifty -0.82%, Bank Nifty -1.04%) indicating domestic headwinds. A weaker rupee (USD/INR 92.98, +0.59%) and higher US 10‑year yields (4.94%, +1.82%) raise funding costs and pressure financials. Sectoral resilience – IT (+1.71%), Metal (+2.59%) and a falling India VIX (-6.37%) point to selective upside and lower volatility.

What to watch

  • US non‑farm payrolls and the Fed minutes for clues on the direction of the 10‑year yield.
  • RBI policy meeting outcomes and any change in repo rate expectations.
  • Nifty IT earnings releases to confirm whether the sector’s recent strength can be sustained.
  • Movements in the USD/INR exchange rate as a barometer of external funding pressures.
  • Gold price trends, given its impact on investor sentiment and the rupee’s safe‑haven appeal.
